title: What Is a Micro-Influencer? Definition, Pay and Why Brands Use Them (2026)
excerpt: What a micro-influencer is, how micro, nano and macro influencers compare, why brands work with them, how they get paid, and how to become one.
content:
What is a micro-influencer?

Quick answer: a micro-influencer is a creator with a mid-sized, focused audience, usually defined as roughly 10,000 to 100,000 followers (some marketers use 10,000 to 50,000). They typically post about one niche, like skincare, fitness or home, and their audiences tend to engage more and trust their recommendations, which is why brands use them for product launches, gifting and UGC.

Influencer tiers compared

TierTypical followersStrengths
NanoAbout 1,000 to 10,000Close-knit audience, very affordable, often open to gifting
MicroAbout 10,000 to 100,000Niche focus, strong engagement, reasonable rates
MacroAbout 100,000 to 1 millionLarge reach, more professional production
MegaOver 1 millionMass awareness, highest fees

The thresholds aren't official; agencies and platforms draw the lines slightly differently.

Why do brands work with micro-influencers?

  • Trust: smaller audiences often treat a creator's recommendation like advice from a friend.
  • Niche fit: a brand can reach exactly the people who buy its category.
  • Cost: brands can work with several micro creators for the price of one large account, which spreads risk.
  • Content: micro creators make native-looking videos that brands can reuse as ads.

How do micro-influencers get paid?

  • Paid posts: a fee per post, Reel or TikTok, often with an extra fee for ad usage rights.
  • Gifting: free product, often the start of a relationship with a brand.
  • UGC: payment for videos the brand posts or runs as ads.
  • Affiliate commission: a share of sales through a code or link.
  • Ambassador programs: longer partnerships with product, commission or a monthly fee.

Rates vary widely with niche, engagement, deliverables and usage rights, so there's no single standard price. See how influencers make money.

Micro-influencer vs UGC creator

A micro-influencer posts to their own audience, so reach and engagement matter. A UGC creator makes content for the brand to post or run as ads, so follower count matters much less. Many creators do both.

How to become a micro-influencer

  1. Choose one niche and post consistently.
  2. Make content that's useful or relatable to a specific audience, not everyone.
  3. Reply to comments and build a real community.
  4. Start working with brands early through gifting and UGC, before you hit 10,000 followers.
  5. Pitch brands in your niche every week with specific ideas.

For creators: pitch brands without the busywork

Polly, Newcollab's AI assistant, matches micro creators with brands in their niche and writes each pitch for that brand's product. For brands, Newcollab's performance UGC lets micro creators post about your product while you pay for the views they deliver.

faq.question: How many followers does a micro-influencer have?
faq.answer: Usually about 10,000 to 100,000 followers, though some marketers define it as 10,000 to 50,000. Creators with about 1,000 to 10,000 followers are often called nano-influencers.

faq.question: Do micro-influencers get paid?
faq.answer: Yes. Micro-influencers earn from paid posts, UGC, affiliate commissions and ambassador programs, and many also accept gifted products, especially early on.

faq.question: What is the difference between a nano and a micro-influencer?
faq.answer: Mostly audience size. Nano-influencers usually have about 1,000 to 10,000 followers and micro-influencers about 10,000 to 100,000. Both tend to have engaged, niche audiences.

faq.question: Why do brands prefer micro-influencers?
faq.answer: Their audiences are focused and engaged, they cost less than large accounts, and brands can work with several at once to test what works and reuse the best content as ads.

faq.question: Can you be a micro-influencer with fewer than 10,000 followers?
faq.answer: By most definitions you'd be a nano-influencer, but brands care more about niche fit and content quality than an exact number. Many creators land gifted and paid deals before 10,000 followers.
